power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: This systematic review synthesizes prospective evidence on associations between obesity assessed in young or middle adulthood and subsequent cognitive performance before age 65.

Methods A comprehensive search of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Web of Science identified prospective studies comparing adults with obesity to those of normal weight and assessing cognitive performance, using validated cognitive tests.
Risk of bias was evaluated using ROBINS-E, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Results Among 4,871 records screened, four publications representing three cohorts met the inclusion criteria.

Two publications from Whitehall II reported small negative associations between obesity assessed in adulthood and global cognitive performance, whereas the MIDUS analysis found no longitudinal association for BMI.
A modestly steeper 10-year decline in global cognition was reported among metabolically unhealthy adults with obesity compared with adults of normal weight in Whitehall II.
Findings for executive function and memory were inconsistent and generally small.
One study was judged at high risk of bias and the other three raised some concerns.

Conclusions The available evidence is too sparse, heterogeneous, and methodologically uncertain to establish a meaningful independent association between obesity and cognitive performance before age 65.

Future prospective studies should include cognitive assessment at baseline and repeated follow-up, report standardized effect estimates, use domain-specific cognitive outcomes, address confounding a priori, and assess central adiposity and metabolic health alongside BMI, particularly in younger adults.

Obesity is a major global public health problem, driven by a complex interplay of genetic, behavioral, social, and environmental factors (Silventoinen et al., 2010; Choquet & Meyre, 2011; Swinburn et al., 2011; Thaker, 2017; Phelps et al., 2024).

text.text: Cognition involves the processes of integrating, storing and utilizing information, with key domains including memory, attention and executive functions.

text.text: In this review, we focused on two age groups: young adults (18-45 years) and middle-aged adults (46-64 years).
Although previous systematic reviews have examined associations between obesity and cognition, many have focused on cross-sectional data, limiting consideration of causal and temporal associations.

These reviews report associations between obesity and poorer cognitive performance, affecting both global cognitive function and specific domains such as executive functions and memory (Van den Berg et al., 2009; Fitzpatrick et al., 2013; Hendrikse et al., 2015; Prickett et al., 2015; Favieri et al., 2019).

text.text: Moreover, most included older populations, providing limited evidence on obesity exposure earlier in adulthood and cognitive outcomes before age 65.

We therefore aimed to synthesize prospective evidence on associations between obesity assessed in young or middle adulthood and subsequent global and domain-specific cognitive performance before age 65.
The protocol was developed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) 2015 guidelines (Shamseer et al., 2015).

text.text: Two deviations from the published protocol were made and are reported here transparently: (i) due to the limited number of studies examining cognitive functions before age 50, and to better include both young and middle-aged adults, the age range was expanded to 18-64 years; (ii) to better assess the exposure-outcome association, we evaluated the risk of bias in the articles using the ROBINS-E tool (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies -of Exposures).
The primary objective of this review was to determine whether obesity is associated with poorer cognitive performance in young to middle-aged adults.
We also investigated whether obesity was associated with poorer performance in overall cognitive function or in specific cognitive domains in this age group.
We defined eligibility criteria using the PECOS model, taking into account population, exposure, comparator, outcome, and study design.
• Adult women and men aged 18 to 64 years at the time of anthropometric measurements and assessment of cognitive functions.

• At the start of the study, participants should: have no history or current cognitive impairment, mental disorders (including addiction), chronic illnesses or bariatric surgery; not be taking regular medication that could affect their cognition; not be pregnant; not be on a weight-loss diet.
• Individuals drawn from the general population.
• Adults with obesity according to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ).
Overweight individuals (25.0 ≤ BMI ≤ 29.9) were excluded.
• Compared with adults with normal weight status (18.5 ≤ BMI ≤ 24.9).
• Studies assessing cognitive performance as an outcome using validated cognitive tests.
Both self-reported and examiner-reported assessments of cognitive functions were included.
• Longitudinal studies with a follow-up of at least two years after exposure, or metaanalyses of such studies.
• Articles published in English or French after 1996, following the WHO's 1997 recommendation to use BMI for diagnosing obesity.
• Grey literature, conference abstracts and narrative reviews were excluded.

The search strategy combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms in PubMed) and freetext keywords covering the population, obesity exposure, global and domain-specific cognitive outcomes, and longitudinal study design.

text.text: PubMed, PsycINFO, and Web of Science were searched through August 2024.
Updates were conducted in January 2026 and October 2026 in PubMed only; these updates identified no additional eligible publication.
Elicit was used as a supplementary AI-assisted search tool rather than as a substitute for database searching.
Reference lists of included publications were also screened, and study authors were contacted when information required for eligibility or extraction was missing or unclear.
All search results were imported into Rayyan, a platform designed for collaborative systematic literature reviews.
After removing duplicates, three authors (CS, MCB and SC) screened the articles based on titles and abstracts.
The full text of potentially eligible articles was then assessed to determine eligibility.
When there was disagreement among the authors, consensus was reached through discussion and, where necessary, a fourth author was consulted.
Three authors (CS, MCB and SC) extracted data from each included study into a standardized data extraction table.
In parallel, one of these authors (CS) used Elicit to extract the same data and compared it with the manually extracted data.

The extracted information included: first author's name, year of publication, country of origin of the cohort, years of data collection, duration of followup, sample size, percentage of women, mean age or age range, mean BMI, cognitive tests used, cognitive functions assessed, and results (estimates of association) relevant to the research objectives.
For the qualitative synthesis, we grouped the results according to the cognitive functions assessed (e.g., global cognitive functions, memory, or executive functions).

Given the heterogeneity of the cognitive performance assessed, the variety of cognitive tests used in the included articles and the differences in the adjustment for confounding variables, we did not perform a meta-analysis, but instead provide a structured narrative synthesis of the results.
The results were organized by cognitive domain, with additional attention to study design and risk of bias, to ensure a structured and systematic narrative synthesis.

Risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-E tool (Higgins et al., 2024) which evaluates seven domains, including confounding factors, exposure measurement, participant selection, postexposure interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and the selection of reported outcomes.

text.text: Overall, the available prospective evidence does not support a clear, clinically meaningful independent association between obesity in young or middle adulthood and cognitive performance before age 65.

Across the three studies examining global cognition, the association with obesity appeared specific to obesity assessed in middle, rather than young, adulthood, and was not replicated in the MIDUS cohort (Sabia et al., 2009; Singh-Manoux et al., 2012a; Hartanto et al., 2019).

text.text: This inconsistency, occurring even across cohorts with broadly similar designs, suggests that any true association is not robust across measurement contexts.

text.text: These inconsistencies highlight the complexity of the relationship between obesity and cognitive outcomes and suggest that factors such as metabolic health, duration of obesity, and vulnerabilities in specific cognitive domains might play a critical role in cognitive decline.
At the same time, the current evidence does not allow firm conclusions that obesity itself meaningfully predicts clinically defined cognitive impairment in non-elderly adults.

Other studies report poorer cognition in later midlife among adults with obesity (Elias et al., 2005; Cournot et al., 2006; Wolf et al., 2007), whereas obesity in older adults has been associated with a possible protective effect (Kuo et al., 2006; Fitzpatrick et al., 2009), which suggests that associations depend on age at assessment.

text.text: No prospective studies have examined global cognition in young adults (between 18 and 45 years of age) with obesity.
While much of the existing literature focuses on older populations, where cognitive decline is more commonly observed, young adults are increasingly affected by rising obesity rates.

The inconsistent pattern may reflect differences in exposure measurement, cognitive tests, confounding control, sample composition, or risk of bias; it is also compatible with the absence of a meaningful independent association.
Evidence directly concerning cognitive outcomes in young adulthood was absent, because obesity was sometimes measured at younger ages but cognition was assessed primarily in middle adulthood.
Evidence for executive functioning was sparse and inconsistent.

Lower executive performance in midlife was reported in adults with obesity assessed in middle adulthood or cumulatively over the life course, but this association was no longer significant after joint adjustment for health behaviors and health measures, which suggests that it may partly reflect shared cardiometabolic and behavioral factors (Sabia et al., 2009).

Future studies should use repeated, domain-specific measures and explicitly test bidirectional associations, because executive performance may influence health behavior and adiposity as well as potentially being associated with them.
Research into the association between obesity and memory has yielded mixed findings.
While some studies suggest that the relationship depends on age, metabolic health and lifestyle factors, others report conflicting or null results.

Establishing an independent association between obesity and cognitive functions is challenging.

Despite the aforementioned constraints, this review also has some notable strengths that deserve to be highlighted.

Prior to conducting this review, we performed a systematic literature search in the PROSPERO, PubMed and Cochrane Library databases, which allowed us to identify five systematic reviews on the same topic.

However, these reviews differed in the age range of the populations included, ranging from no restrictions (Van den Berg et al., 2009; Hendrikse et al., 2015) to specific age ranges, such as 5 to 70 years (Favieri et al., 2019) or 18 to 65 years (Fitzpatrick et al., 2013; Prickett et al., 2015).

The review's principal contribution is therefore not to confirm an obesity-cognition association, but to demonstrate how little high-quality prospective evidence currently supports such a conclusion in young and middle-aged adults.

This systematic review highlights that although several studies have found poorer cognitive performance in middle-aged adults with obesity, an independent association remains inconclusive, particularly in young to middle-aged adults.

Given that one of the four included studies was judged at high risk of bias and that findings were inconsistent across cohorts, the current evidence remains too weak to support a robust independent association between obesity and poorer cognitive performance, and the possibility that no true link exists cannot be excluded.

As obesity rates increase at earlier ages, it is crucial to determine whether cognitive functions are impaired and whether such impairment occurs before the onset of typical age-related cognitive decline.

Further research is needed to identify which cognitive domains are most vulnerable to obesity over time, particularly in light of emerging evidence that obesity-related neurodegeneration may mirror processes observed in Alzheimer's disease.

Identifying these high-risk domains may allow the development of targeted interventions-such as dietary changes, physical activity or bariatric surgery-to preserve or improve cognition in adults with obesity.

Ultimately, this may help prevent cognitive impairment from preventing individuals with obesity from adopting and maintaining healthy behaviors, while potentially reducing the risk of dementia in later life.
Future research should identify which cognitive domains are particularly vulnerable to obesity in young adults, helping to guide early, targeted interventions.
To achieve this, prospective studies should incorporate relevant control variables such as age, education, and depression, use appropriate control groups, and consider both BMI and WHR.
Nevertheless, these design improvements are necessary before implications for prevention or intervention can be justified.
